en: *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, Chapter on Refutation through Counter-Interrogation, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter One: Illogical Objections within the Chapter on Refutation through Counter-Interrogation. *Yùdàolì nànpǐn* (The Section on Illogical Objections). First.
The treatise says:
You claim that my speech is illogical;
if that were so, your own speech would likewise be illogical.
If your statement is unreasonable, then my statement is reasonable.
If your statement is reasonable, yet you claim my statement is unreasonable, that is not the case.
Furthermore, that which is irrational possesses rationality within its own nature; therefore, there is no such thing as the irrational.
If there were no rationality within its own nature, then the irrational would likewise not exist. Thus, your claim that "I am irrational" is incorrect.
Furthermore, if you claim that my speech lacks reason, this only reveals your own lack of wisdom.
Why is this? That which lacks reason is non-existent; is your speech then identical to or different from that which lacks reason?
If they were identical, there would be no verbal expression at all; why then do you claim that my verbal expression is illogical?
If they were different, verbal expression would possess logic; why then do you further claim that my verbal expression is illogical?
Furthermore, because verbal expression contradicts its own intrinsic nature:
when you challenge my verbal expression with your own, do they occur simultaneously or not simultaneously?
If they are simultaneous, then they cannot refute my verbal expression; for example, just as the horns of a cow and the ears of a horse arise simultaneously and thus cannot refute one another.
If they were not simultaneous, your objection would come first and my statement would follow; since my statement had not yet been uttered, what would you have had to object to?
Therefore, your objection is invalid.
If my statement comes first and your objection comes later, my statement is already established; what, then, is there left to object to?

If they were simultaneous, it would be impossible to distinguish between my statement and your objection, or between the objection and the object of the objection—just as when the waters of a river and the waters of the ocean merge simultaneously, they cannot be distinguished.
Furthermore, does your objection refute your own position or not?
If it refutes your own position, your own position is undermined by itself, and my argument is thereby established.
If it does not refute your own position, then your objection fails to be established.
Why is this? Because the objection is not established within one's own position.
If it were established, one's own position would be destroyed and the opponent's position would be proven.

Furthermore, as for your claim that my speech lacks reason, it would not be speech at all; if it is speech, it cannot lack reason. To say there is speech and yet it lacks reason is a contradiction between these two.
For example, it is like a maiden who has a son. If she is a maiden, she cannot have a son;
if she has a son, she is not a maiden.
These two states—being a maiden and having a son—are contradictory. Therefore, to claim that such a statement is illogical is incorrect.
Furthermore, because it contradicts realized knowledge (*pramāṇa-jñāna*):
if you have heard my words and yet claim they are unreasonable, then by the very fact that you have heard them, they are established by realized knowledge.
The power of realized knowledge (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) is great; thus, your statement is refuted.

For example, if someone were to say that sound is not apprehended by auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), [we would reply that] since auditory consciousness does indeed apprehend sound, it is established by realized knowledge.
The statement that "the power of the knowledge of realization is great" would then be undermined.
Furthermore, because it contradicts inferential knowledge (*anumāna*).
If you claim that I have made such a statement, then one would know through inferential knowledge that there is indeed a logical basis for it.
If there were no underlying principle, there would be no discourse;
if there is discourse, one knows that a principle exists.
For example, it is like someone saying that sound is eternal because it arises from causes.
All things that arise from causes are not permanent; for example, because a clay vessel arises from causes, it cannot be permanent.
If sound were to arise from causes, it could not be permanent;
if it were permanent, it could not have arisen from causes.
That which is not eternally abiding is established by inferential knowledge (*anumāna*).
Because the power of inferential knowledge is great, that which is eternally abiding is sublated.

Regarding that which possesses logical consistency: if there is a verbal expression, there is logical consistency; that which possesses logical consistency is established by inferential knowledge, while that which lacks logical consistency is sublated.
Furthermore, because it contradicts worldly convention:
you claim that my statement is irrational, yet this very statement contradicts worldly convention. Why is this so?
Within the world, four kinds of principles are established:
first, the principle of cause and effect; second, the principle of mutual dependence; third, the principle of accomplishment; and fourth, the principle of suchness.
The principle of cause and effect is like that of a seed and its sprout.
The principle of mutual dependence is like that of long and short, or father and son.
The principle of establishment is like the meaning established by the five-membered syllogism.
Regarding the principle of suchness (*tathatā*), there are three kinds:
first, the suchness of selflessness; second, the suchness of impermanence; and third, the suchness of tranquility.

In the world, conventional expression is said to be the effect and the principle to be the cause; thus, if one perceives an effect in the world, one knows that a cause exists, and if one perceives conventional expression, one knows that a principle exists.
You claim that my words lack reason, but this argument contradicts common worldly understanding.
It is impossible for there to be speech that lacks reason.
You claim that my statement is inconsistent and therefore erroneous; I shall now debate this point with you to reach a definitive conclusion: if one speaks inconsistently, there is a fault.
If your own established thesis differs from my thesis, then it is your own statement and it is a divergent statement; therefore, you incur the fault.
If your thesis differs from what I have stated, then the fault of divergence lies with you and does not concern me.
If they were not different, you would be the same as me, and thus there would be no difference; yet you claim that I am different, which is a false statement.
Furthermore, difference and difference are themselves non-different; therefore, there is no difference.
If difference were different from difference, then it would not be difference.
For example, if a person is different from an ox, the person is not the ox.
If difference were not different from difference, then they would be one; if they were one, there would be no difference. Why, then, do you say that I am different?
Furthermore, as for this principle: because I dispute with you regarding your principle, I maintain that there is a difference.
If you were not different from me, then I would not dispute with you, as I would be stating your own position.
If all that you have said is different [from what I have said], then you too have something to say; therefore, since you claim there is a difference, the fault lies with you.
If you say that you do not state anything different, then I likewise do not state anything different.
Your claim that I have stated something different is incorrect; your words are erroneous.
The remaining points are as previously explained.
You assert that my argument is unestablished; I shall now debate this matter with you to reach a definitive resolution.
If you say it is unestablished, that is a statement of its being unestablished.
If that which is stated is unestablished, then it cannot be stated.
If it cannot be stated, how can you state that what I have said is unestablished?
If [a statement] could be established, then what is stated would be proven.
Since you claim it is not proven, your position is incorrect.
If all that is stated were unproven, then the objection you raise against me would itself be unproven.
If you say that my objection is not unestablished, I say that it is likewise not unestablished.
Your claim that my [objection] is unestablished is incorrect.
Non-attainment is established within its own essence; therefore, there is no such thing as non-attainment.
If non-attainment were not established within its own essence, then non-attainment itself would likewise not exist.
If there is accomplishment, then there is no non-accomplishment; therefore, your claim that I am not accomplished is untenable.

If you say that by not reciting my objection you fail to grasp my meaning, and if you fail to grasp my meaning you cannot effectively challenge me, I shall now engage you in a definitive debate on this point.
If you have not recited my objection, then you cannot state your own objection.
Do you state your objection after having recited the objection, or do you state it without having recited it?
If you are able to state an objection without having recited it, then I too am able to state an objection without having recited it.
If you recite that "the objection is difficult to state," then you will always be reciting the objection. Why is this?

Because within the objection another objection arises, and thus objections would be infinite; there would never be a time when one does not recite an objection, nor a time when one is able to state an objection.
Furthermore, from one name for an objection there arises another name for an objection.

If one must recite the name of an objection in order to state that objection, and cannot state it without such recitation, then one could only recite the preceding objection’s name after having already stated the subsequent one; one would not be able to recite the second objection’s name until after the third, nor the third objection’s name until after the fourth. In this manner, one would be reciting them endlessly.
If you can state the name of a challenge without having recited it now, then the name of the first challenge should also be able to be stated without having been recited.
If the name of the first challenge cannot be stated without having been recited, then the second challenge should likewise be able to be stated without having its name recited;
and if the second can be stated without its name being recited, then the first should also be able to be stated without its name being recited.

Now, regarding the first objection (*dūsana*), one must necessarily recite its name before being able to state that objection; likewise, for the second objection, one should also necessarily recite its name before being able to state it, rather than stating it without having recited it.

Furthermore, if one states a challenge without having recited the opponent's challenge, one falls into a point of defeat; since you have not recited your own challenge, your statement of a challenge likewise falls into a point of defeat.

If, however, stating a challenge without having recited the challenge does not constitute a point of defeat for you, then I too shall state a challenge without having recited the challenge, and I likewise shall not fall into a point of defeat.
Furthermore, if you say that you will recite all my objections when I speak them,
and I shall likewise recite all your objections when you raise them against me—
such that we can only mutually recite one another's words— then it would be impossible for either of us to establish an independent objection.
If one were to constantly recite [the words] while maintaining their mutual connection, the correct meaning would be lost.
It is like two boats tied together; when a great flood arrives, they are pulled back and forth by it.
Furthermore, you claim that all these are merely sounds which perish as soon as they leave the mouth; how, then, could my words be recited?
Since sound is a phenomenon that perishes and cannot be restored, it cannot be recited again.
If the sound were still present, one could not recite it, because it would be a constant sound;
if it has perished, there is nothing to recite, because it no longer exists.
If the sound has already perished, yet you claim that I am reciting it by asserting "this is your speech," this is a false conception.
You say that my words contradict themselves; I shall now debate with you to resolve this matter.
If I were to say that my former statement refutes your later one, this would be logical. Why?
Because my statement comes first and yours comes later; if my statement refutes your later statement, then my position prevails and your statement is invalidated.
Furthermore, if you claim that every preceding statement refutes what follows, then your own speech should also refute what follows it.
If your preceding speech does not refute what follows, then my preceding speech likewise does not refute what follows.
Furthermore, regarding the case where the prior negates the posterior: within its own essence, there is no prior negating the posterior.
If there were a prior negating the posterior within its own essence, then both the prior and the posterior would be non-existent.
Therefore, your statement that the former refutes the latter is incorrect.
If, within its own essence, there is no prior refuting of what follows because of the absence of a cause, then the prior refuting of the subsequent is likewise non-existent.
Your claim that my previous statement refutes the subsequent one is a false reflection.
You say that I have stated a different reason; I shall now debate this point with you.
If a person incurs a point of defeat by abandoning a prior reason and establishing a different reason, then you yourself have fallen into that point of defeat.
Why is this? Because you also abandon the previous reason and establish a different one.
If your establishment of a different reason does not constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), then the same applies to me as well.
Furthermore, the reason I have stated differs from the reason you have stated.
If I were to state a different reason, that would constitute my own logical position.
If I do not state a different reason, I am merely stating your own reason; it would not be a counter-argument or a contradiction, but would simply be identical to what you have said.
Your claim that I have stated a different reason is a false conception.
If I were to establish a reason identical to yours and you were to refute my reason, you would thereby refute your own reason as well.
Furthermore, if every utterance constitutes a distinct reason (*hetu*), then your own utterance would likewise constitute a distinct reason; therefore, you fall into defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
If your utterance does not result in defeat, then your claim that my proposed reason results in defeat is untenable.
If you claim that I am stating a different meaning, I shall now debate and resolve this point with you.
That my established position differs from yours is precisely the logical principle.
My position now stands in opposition to yours; therefore, I shall state a different meaning.
If you consider my meaning to be no different from yours, then my meaning would not stand in opposition to yours. If you were to refute my meaning, you would be refuting yourself.
Furthermore, if the concept of difference does not exist within its own essence, then the concept of difference is non-existent.
If the concept of difference were to exist within its own essence, even then the concept of difference would be non-existent.
Therefore, your claim that I am propounding a different meaning is incorrect.
Furthermore, if everything that is spoken constitutes a different meaning, then what you yourself have said must also constitute a different meaning.
If you have something to say that does not constitute a different meaning, yet you claim that everything said constitutes a different meaning, this position is untenable.
As for your claim that my current speech is identical to my previous speech and that there is no difference between them, I shall now engage with you in a formal debate to resolve this matter.
My established thesis contradicts and opposes yours; if I were to state my own thesis as a counter-argument to yours, that would be the correct principle. Why is this so?
I have stated in every instance that this is for the purpose of refuting your position; therefore, I say there is no difference.
If I were to state a different meaning, then your established thesis would differ from my own.

If I were to state a different meaning, then I would be stating your own meaning; in that case, there would be no contradiction with you, and your objection to me would be an objection to your own position.

Furthermore, as I previously stated that sound is impermanent, this statement itself perishes and ceases of its own accord. To now produce a separate statement and claim that I am repeating my previous words is a false conception.

Furthermore, if you say that what I have stated is not different [from what you intend], then if I were to state it as different, it would indeed be different; and if I were to state it as non-different, it would indeed be non-different.
If my statement cannot be established, then your claim that "I am non-different" is incorrect. This meaning is not so.
If you say, "I do not accept anything that has been said," I shall now debate this point with you.
When you say you do not accept anything, does this statement itself fall within the category of "everything" or does it not?
If you include [this position] within all categories of enumeration, then you yourself do not accept what you have asserted.
If you do not accept it yourself, then my thesis is what you have accepted; thus, my thesis is established and your statement is refuted.
If that which does not enter into any enumeration were non-existent, then there would be nothing at all.
If there were nothing at all, you would not admit anything.
If you do not admit anything, my thesis is not what you have denied; thus my thesis is established and your statement is ultimately refuted.
Chapter Two: Objections Based on Reasoning (*yukti-dūṣaṇa*) within the Chapter on Counter-Objections. The Treatise says: There are three kinds of faults in an objection:

first, the inverted objection; second, the objection based on non-factual meaning; and third, the contradictory objection. If an objection possesses these three kinds of faults, it falls into a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
First, the "inverted objection" (*viparīta-ākṣepa*): when one formulates an objection that does not correspond to the correct meaning, it is called an inverted objection.
There are ten types of inverted objections:

(1) the objection based on similarity (*sādharmya-ākṣepa*), (2) the objection based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-ākṣepa*), (3) the objection based on extension (*atiprasaṅga-ākṣepa*), (4) the objection of non-difference (*aviśeṣa-ākṣepa*), (5) the objection of reaching or not reaching (*prāptyaprāpti-ākṣepa*), (6) the objection of lack of cause (*ahetu-ākṣepa*), (7) the objection of revealing a distinct cause (*kāraṇāntara-ākṣepa*), (8) the objection of doubt (*saṃśaya-ākṣepa*), (9) the objection of what has not been stated (*anuktā-ākṣepa*), and (10) the objection of difference in the matter (*arthāntara-ākṣepa*).
1. The Objection based on Similarity (*sādharmya-khaṇḍana*): To raise an objection by means of a similarity with the object [of the thesis] is called the objection based on similarity.
The treatise says:

Sound is impermanent because it arises from effort (*puruṣakāra*), since there is no interval between its arising [and its destruction]; for example, a clay pot arises from effort and, having arisen, is destroyed.
Sound is also like this; therefore, the proposition that sound is impermanent is established.
The opponent says:
If sound is impermanent and shares the same characteristics as material objects, then sound must be permanent, because it shares the same characteristics as space.
Therefore, as with space, sound is also eternal, because they share the same characteristic of being without a physical body.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, sound is impermanent because it arises from effort and does not arise without an interval.
If a thing were eternal, it would not arise from effort, just as space is eternal and does not arise from effort.
Sound is not like this; therefore, sound is impermanent. This point is established.
The opponent says:
If sound is impermanent because it has characteristics different from the eternally abiding space, then what follows?
If it has characteristics identical to space, then sound is eternal.
That which has the same characteristic is bodiless; therefore, it is eternal.
The Treatise says:
Both of these challenges are erroneous and fail to constitute valid objections.

Why is this? Because the principle of a single, determinate flavor (*ekarasa*) is established as the cause, it reveals that all things are impermanent, arising through the power of causes and conditions.

This demonstrates that the cause of impermanence is determinately of a single flavor; therefore, impermanence is unshakeable. To reveal its commonality with other instances, the analogies of clay pots and the like are cited.
The opponent raises an objection based on the lack of a definitive single flavor in external reliance, saying:
"If you establish the meaning of sound's impermanence based on its common characteristics, I too shall establish the meaning of sound's permanence based on those same common characteristics."
If your thesis is established, my thesis is also established.
The commentary says:
Your objection is invalid.
Why is this? Your established reason (*hetu*) is not determinate, because it is pervasively manifested as both permanent and impermanent.

My established reason possesses the three characteristics as its fundamental properties: it is subsumed by the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and excluded from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); therefore, my established reason is accomplished and unshakable.
Your reason is not valid; therefore, your objection is inverted.
If you were to establish a reason identical to my reason, then your objection would constitute a valid objection.
If one who posits impermanence as their thesis objects to the thesis of permanence, that objection is established.
Why is this? Because establishing a permanent cause is difficult.

Establishing an impermanent cause cannot effectively reveal the fault of the inversion regarding impermanence; for a permanent cause is not of a single, determinate nature, whereas an impermanent cause is of a single, determinate nature.

2. The Objection Based on Different Characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa-khaṇḍana*): To raise an objection by positing that the characteristics of an object are different [from those of the probandum] is called the objection based on different characteristics.
The treatise says:
"Sound is impermanent."
Why is this? Because they are produced by causes and conditions.
If any thing arises in dependence upon causes and conditions, it is impermanent, just like space.
Space is eternal and does not arise dependent upon causes and conditions.
Sound is not like this; therefore, sound is impermanent.
The opponent says:
If sound is impermanent because its characteristics differ from those of eternal space, then to what end is it impermanent?
If its characteristics differ from those of a clay pot, then sound must be eternal.
Regarding their differing characteristics: sound is incorporeal, whereas a clay vessel is corporeal; therefore, the clay vessel is impermanent, while sound is permanent.
The treatise states:
Sound is impermanent because it arises dependent upon causes and conditions. For example, just as a clay vessel is impermanent because it arises dependent upon causes and conditions, so too is sound.
The opponent says:
If you establish that sound is impermanent because it shares the same characteristics as a clay pot, what follows from this?
Sound must be permanent, because it does not share the same characteristics as a clay pot.
Regarding their differing characteristics: sound is incorporeal, whereas a clay vessel is corporeal.
The treatise states:
both of these objections are inverted.
Why is this? I establish impermanence because its cause is determined to be of a single flavor;
you establish permanence because its cause is not determined to be of a single flavor, as both permanence and impermanence are manifested pervasively.
Therefore, an inconclusive reason cannot refute a conclusive reason.

The reason I establish is that sound is impermanent because it arises dependent on causes and conditions; this reason constitutes the fundamental property (*dharmatā*), is subsumed within the similar class, and is excluded from the dissimilar class. Because it possesses these three characteristics (*trairūpya*), it is unshakable.

The reason you have established—that sound is eternal because it lacks a body—is subsumed under both the similar and dissimilar classes regarding the fundamental property; therefore, it does not constitute a valid reason.

3. Regarding the objection based on the characteristic of extension (*vyāpakaviśeṣa-dūṣaṇa*): To manifest a specific characteristic within a general characteristic is called the objection based on the characteristic of extension.
The treatise says:
Sound is impermanent because it arises from effort, just like a clay pot; therefore, sound is impermanent.
The opponent says:
You establish that sound shares the same characteristics as a clay vessel because both are produced through effort;
yet there are other distinctions: first, one can be baked while the other cannot; second, one is visible to the eye while the other is not, and so forth.

Thus, there are distinct reasons for the sound and the earthen vessel respectively: the sound arises from effort and is eternal, whereas the earthen vessel arises from effort and is impermanent; therefore, the sound is eternal.
The treatise says:
This objection is inverted. Why is this so?

I have established that my reason (*hetu*) is inseparable from impermanence and separate from permanence; this demonstrates that the reason serves as an inference for impermanence. It is, for example, like smoke being manifested as an inference for fire: smoke is inseparable from fire. Therefore, the reason I have established is proven and unshakable.

If you claim that sound is eternal because it cannot be burned or cooked, then desire, hatred, suffering, pleasure, wind, and so forth also cannot be burned or cooked, yet they are impermanent; therefore, the fact of being incapable of being burned or cooked cannot be established as a reason for eternity.
That which is not seen by the eye cannot be established as a permanent cause.
Why? Because desire, hatred, suffering, pleasure, wind, and so forth are also not seen by the eye, yet they are impermanent.
Your reason is subsumed within both similar and dissimilar classes; therefore, it is not established.
If your reason were identical to my reason, you would be able to refute my thesis;
however, my thesis relies upon a reason characterized by the three marks, and for that reason, they are not the same.
To claim that what is different is the same is a perverted objection; therefore, your critique is inverted.

Fourth, the "objection of non-difference" (aviśeṣa-jāti): because it demonstrates that a single common characteristic exists, it establishes that there is no reason for everything [to be distinct]; this is called the objection of non-difference.
The treatise says:

Sound is impermanent because it varies according to its causes and conditions; as sound itself varies—just as, for example, a lamp’s flame is large when the wick is large and small when the wick is small—this principle is established.
The opponent says:
If, by relying on common characteristics, jars and other such things are impermanent and sound is likewise so, then all things would be no different from one another.
Why is this? Because all things share common characteristics with other things.
What are these common characteristics?
That which is "knowable" and so forth is called a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

If there were such a common characteristic, then while all things would differ from other things, sound would likewise share common characteristics with objects such as earthenware jars; yet sound is eternal, whereas earthenware jars and the like are impermanent.

Why is this? Because within the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of all things being "existent" and so forth, there exists a difference in intrinsic nature (svabhāva); thus, like a lamp, sound, a person, or a horse, if one were to infer based on a common characteristic, it would not be established.
The treatise says:
This objection is inverted. Why is this so?
Regarding all things, there exists a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which I do not discard.

However, having examined their specific differences, I establish the meaning of impermanence based on that which possesses the three characteristics; I declare this to be the reason for impermanence, rather than taking the mere common characteristic alone.
If one does not investigate and discern the principle in this manner, then there is no distinct principle whatsoever. Why is this?
Because there is not a single thing that is not different from or distinct from other things.
Therefore, if there is a common characteristic (*sādharmya*), it is subsumed under the same class and is entirely distinct from other classes.
If one takes this as the established reason (*hetu*), that reason is valid.
If one establishes a reason based solely on similarity (*sādharmya*), it is not established; therefore, it is erroneous.
Furthermore, the treatise says:
Sound is impermanent because it arises dependent upon causes and conditions, just like a clay pot and so forth; therefore, sound is impermanent.
The opponent says:
There is no difference between the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*). Why is this?
What is the meaning of "arising based on causes"?
It means that as long as the causes have not yet come together, the sound has not yet arisen; because it has not yet arisen, it does not exist—this is its meaning.
What is the meaning of "sound is impermanent"?

The meaning is that sound, which had not yet arisen, attains arising; having arisen, it immediately ceases. Because it has ceased, it does not exist. This is because the reason (*hetu*) is identical to the thesis (*pakṣa*) in its non-existence.
The treatise says:
"This objection is inverted."
Why is this? The non-existence established by me is the non-existence of destruction;
the non-existence established by me as the reason is the non-existence of that which has not yet arisen.
The non-existence of that which has not yet arisen is established as a cause for impermanence because it is widely accepted by most people in the world;

however, the non-existence resulting from destruction is not established because the Sāṃkhyas and others do not accept it, and thus it is posited as a logical argument (artha) in order to establish [the former].
If you establish a thesis based on what is unestablished and take that which is unestablished as the reason, then your objection is superior and not erroneous.

I maintain that all things did not exist prior to their arising and are seen not to exist after they have ceased; therefore, sound did not exist prior to its arising, and it likewise does not exist after its cessation.
If you do not believe that there was no sound in previous lives, reflect for yourself: if there were sound in previous lives and it were unimpeded, why did the ear not hear it?
Therefore, you should know that what did not exist in previous lives is like the feet of a snake.
If someone, out of a competitive spirit, cannot accomplish the intended meaning, and though they wish to accomplish it, there is no logical way to do so, such a position should be abandoned.
5. The objection regarding "reaching" (*prāpti*) and "not reaching" (*aprāpti*): Does the reason reach the thesis (*sādhya*) or not reach it?
If the reason reaches it, the reason cannot establish the thesis;
if the reason does not reach it, the reason likewise cannot establish the thesis. This is called the objection regarding reaching and not reaching.
The opponent says:

If the reason arrives [at the thesis] such that it is identical with or mixed with the thesis to be established, then the thesis is not established. For example, when river water enters the ocean, there is no longer any river water; the reason is likewise, and therefore it does not constitute a valid reason.
If the thesis to be established has not yet been accomplished, the reason cannot reach it.
If it has reached it, the thesis to be established is already accomplished; what, then, would be the use of the reason?
Therefore, the reason is unestablished.
If the reason does not reach the thesis to be established, it is like other things that cannot function as a reason; therefore, the reason is unestablished.
If the reason does not reach its object, it has no efficacy, just as fire that does not reach its object cannot burn, and a sword that does not reach its object cannot cut.
The treatise says:
This objection is inverted.
There are two kinds of causes:
First is the cause of production; second is the cause of manifesting inseparability.
Your objection would be valid if it were based on the cause of production, but if it is based on the cause of manifestation, it is a misconception.

Why is this? I state the reason (*hetu*) not for the sake of producing the thesis (*pakṣa*) that has already been established, but so that others may gain conviction; it serves to demonstrate that the thesis is not dissociated from what is to be proven, for the thesis already exists.
Within the establishment of the thesis (*pratijñā*), if the cognition corresponding to the object has not yet arisen, why is this?
It is because of ignorance; therefore, it is said that the cause serves to manifest [the object], just as when color already exists, a lamp is used to manifest it rather than to produce it.
Therefore, the objection regarding the cause of arising is a perverted objection within the context of the manifest cause.

Sixth, the objection regarding the absence of a cause (*ahetuvāda*) consists in asserting that there is no cause throughout the three periods of time; this is called the objection regarding the absence of a cause.
The opponent says:
Does the reason exist prior to the thesis to be established, posterior to it, or simultaneous with it?
If the reason exists in a prior time and the thesis to be established exists in a subsequent time, then since the thesis does not yet exist, what could the reason be a reason for?
If the subsequent effect exists while the established thesis (the cause) exists in a prior time, then since the thesis is already accomplished, what further use would there be for a cause?

If they were to arise simultaneously within the same time-period, they could not be related as cause and effect; for example, when a cow's horns or a seed and its sprout exist at one and the same time, one cannot say that the left produces the right. Therefore, where things are simultaneous, there is no causal relationship.
The treatise says:
This objection is inverted. Why is this so?
That which has already arisen in a previous existence arises depending on causes; it is like lighting a lamp to reveal an object already present, not to produce an object that does not yet exist.
You use the cause of arising to challenge my reason for manifestation; this challenge is inverted and therefore untenable.
If you raise this objection:
"If this is a manifest cause, then since wisdom does not yet exist when this cause is present, of what would this cause be the cause?
Therefore, it cannot be established as a manifest cause."
If one raises such an objection, the cause has not yet obtained its name so long as the effect does not exist.
Once the effect exists, it then obtains the name "cause.

This [cause] is that which manifests the effect; at that time it obtains the name "cause. Thus, the statement implies that it had not obtained the name "cause" previously, and only subsequently does it obtain the name "cause."
If it is said that the cause precedes and the effect follows, then there is no fault.
Someone may raise this objection:
"If this is the case, then the effect does not arise from the cause."
This also does not constitute a valid objection. Why?

Because that preceding entity receives the name "cause" only with respect to what follows; if the entity had already ceased before the subsequent event arose, then this objection would be established.
Since this is not the case, there was no name for it prior, and only subsequently did it receive a name; therefore, the effect arises from a cause.

Seventh, the "objection based on the manifestation of a distinct cause" (*viśeṣahetu-dūṣaṇa*): because an impermanent phenomenon is manifested by relying on a distinct cause, that [distinct cause] is not the [actual] cause; this is called the objection based on the manifestation of a distinct cause.
The opponent says:

If sound is impermanent because it depends on effort (*puruṣakāra*), then that which occurs without effort should be permanent. However, things such as lightning, wind, and so forth, though not produced by effort, are nonetheless subsumed under impermanence. Therefore, establishing impermanence does not require dependence on effort, for effort is not the cause [of impermanence].

If it were a cause, then impermanence would not exist elsewhere apart from effort; for example, smoke cannot be established apart from fire, as smoke is the direct cause of fire and is never dissociated from it.
Efficient power (*śakti*) is not like this; therefore, it does not constitute a valid reason (*hetu*).
Furthermore, efficient power cannot establish the meaning of impermanence. Why is that?
Because it is not pervasive, it arises through effort and power.
If it were pervasive, one could establish its impermanence; if it were not pervasive, one could not establish its impermanence.
For example, suppose someone were to propose this thesis:
All trees possess consciousness. Why is this?
Because trees are able to sleep, just like the śirīṣa tree.
Someone raises an objection, saying:
"The consciousness of a tree deity is not established. Why is this?"
Because it is not pervasive.
When one śirīṣa tree is dormant, other trees are not; thus, this dormancy does not pervade all trees. Therefore, dormancy cannot establish that all trees possess conscious sentience.
The same applies to that which arises through effort (*puruṣakāra*): because it does not pervade all impermanent things, it cannot establish [the universal nature of] impermanence.
The Treatise says:

This objection is inverted; my statement is not like this. I do not say that arising through effort is the cause capable of manifesting the impermanence of *all* things, while other causes are incapable.
If there were another reason capable of manifesting impermanence, I would indeed rejoice, for my own thesis would then be established.
Since the reason I have established is capable of manifesting it, and other reasons are likewise capable of manifesting it, the point I have asserted is proven.
For example, just as fire is known by means of smoke, if one says that fire is also established by seeing its light, my position is likewise:
impermanence is manifested through the power of effort; if there were another cause capable of manifesting impermanence, the meaning of impermanence would still be established.
Therefore, your objection is inverted, for it does not challenge my position as intended.
If I were to say that all impermanent things arise based on effort, you might then object:
"Because arising based on effort is not universal, this reason is unestablished."
This objection is superior.

I state that whatever has sound and so forth produced through effort and power is entirely impermanent; I do not state that all impermanent things are produced through effort and power. Therefore, your objection is inverted.
8. The Objection Based on Doubt (*saṃśaya-jāti*): This refers to raising an objection regarding a common characteristic among heterogeneous classes.
The treatise states:
"Sound is impermanent because it arises from effort."
If there is an entity that arises dependent upon effort and power, that entity is impermanent, just like a clay pot; this principle has already been established.

The opponent says: "That which has already arisen is manifested dependent upon effort and power, just as roots, water, and so forth are manifested dependent upon effort and power; it is not that they arise dependent upon effort and power."
Sound is also like this; therefore, the reason based on "effort" (*puruṣakāra*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it exists both before and after production.
Consequently, based on this reason, doubt arises regarding sound: "What is the definitive nature of this sound?"
Is it like a clay vessel that has not yet arisen and now comes into being, or is it like roots and water that already exist and merely become manifest?
Therefore, it is not certain.
If one raises doubt based on the cause of its arising, one should know that this is not a valid reason for establishing a thesis.
Why is this? Because it can produce and manifest [them].
The treatise says:
This objection is inverted. Why?
Because I do not say that sound is manifested through effort; I say that sound is produced through effort. Therefore, sound is impermanent.
What is your objection?
If you say that the effects of causal efficiency are of two kinds— first, production,
and second, manifestation— then [we respond as follows].
"Produced" refers to things such as clay pots;
"manifested" refers to things such as roots and water.
Sound is a product of effort (*puruṣakāra*); therefore, regarding it, there arises doubt as to whether it is permanent or impermanent.
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because the sense faculties, water, and so forth are not things produced by deliberate effort.
If you say that the sense organs and water perform the function of manifesting [the object], this does not contradict my position. Why?
Because that which has not yet arisen depends upon causal power to arise.
Therefore, since the product of effort (*puruṣakāra*) is of one kind and is likewise impermanent, your objection is invalid.

Furthermore, if you were to demonstrate that the product of effort is of two kinds of impermanence—namely, that the arising of a clay vessel is impermanent while the cessation of the clay vessel is permanent—and that sound is likewise so.
This doubt is also not tenable. Why?
Because it is not established.
If the clay vessel were to cease while existing within that cessation, then because it exists therein, the meaning of "cessation" would not exist.
If it does not exist within that cessation, then there is no such thing as cessation.
Why is this? Because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If you say it is like darkness—where darkness exists because there is no light within it—then [the same logic applies].
The same applies to cessation (*nirodha*): because there is nothing within cessation, it exists as cessation.
This interpretation is incorrect; for if things such as flowers in the sky, the son of a barren woman, or the horns of a rabbit do not exist, they would [absurdly] have to exist.
If you do not admit that things such as flowers in the sky exist, then the same applies to the destruction of a clay vessel; it cannot be said to exist.
Therefore, since the nature of being produced by effort is identical in both cases, they are equally impermanent; thus, your doubt is unfounded.
Because you do not believe, I shall cause you to gain faith.
Therefore, I have stated that sound is impermanent due to its having a cause. Why is this so?
Because sound is manifested through effort and power without obstruction from previous lives, one knows that sound does not exist [as a substantial entity], just like a clay vessel.
You have established two distinct meanings for "obtained through effort and power" and "produced by effort and power."
This interpretation is not correct.
What is the correct meaning?
That which is obtained through effort and exertion is invariably impermanent.
Why is this? Because that which has not yet arisen comes into being, and that which has already arisen ceases.
Therefore, the sense faculties, water, and so forth are likewise impermanent; what need is there for you to establish that manifestation (*vyakta*) is permanent?
9. The Objection of the Unstated (*apratyukta-ākṣepa*): Before it has been stated, impermanence does not yet exist; this is called the objection of the unstated.
The Commentary says:
The meaning is fundamentally as before.
The opponent says:
If it is asserted that sound is impermanent because its cause is effortful speech, then what follows?
It follows that before the occurrence of effortful speech, sound is permanent; this is the logical consequence.
If the sound of the previous life was already permanent, how could it now be impermanent?
The treatise says:
This objection is inverted.
Why is this? I establish causes in order to clarify meaning, not for the sake of arising and not for the sake of ceasing.
If my establishment of causes were subject to destruction, then your critique would be superior.
If you challenge me by claiming that I have not yet stated or established the impermanence of sound, that challenge is "similar" (sādharmya-sama);
if you challenge me by using the cause of destruction, that challenge is "contradictory" (viparīta-sama).

10. The Objection Based on the Difference in Nature (*arthāntara-dūṣaṇa*): Because the nature of the thing is different; for example, a clay pot [is impermanent], whereas sound is not like this. This is called the objection based on the difference in nature. The treatise says:
"Sound is impermanent because it arises dependent upon causes and conditions, just like a clay pot. This argument has already been established.
The opponent says:
Sound is a distinct entity; a clay vessel is a distinct entity.
Since they are distinct entities, they cannot both equally be impermanent.
The treatise says:
This objection is inverted. Why is this so?

I do not say that sound is impermanent because it shares the same function as a vessel; rather, I say that all things are impermanent because they arise based on common causes. This has nothing to do with sharing the same function. For example, like a clay jar, sound is therefore impermanent.
Smoke is a distinct entity yet can manifest fire; likewise, a clay vessel can manifest that sound is impermanent.
Furthermore, another person offers a counter-objection based on the difference between things, stating that sound is eternal because it depends upon space (*ākāśa*), and space is eternal.
If there were a separate entity that depended upon space, that entity would be eternal, just as, for example, the spherical atom (*paramāṇu*) is.
Since the spherical atom is eternal, whatever depends upon the spherical atom must likewise be eternal.
Sound is likewise: because it depends upon space, it is eternally abiding.
Furthermore, sound is eternally abiding. Why is this?
Because it is apprehended by the ear, just as the nature of sound—whether identical or different—is apprehended by the ear and is therefore permanent, so too is sound;
thus it is permanent. This is the formulation of the counter-argument.
The Vaiśeṣika says:
"If that which is permanent were established by means of a cause, then because it would be dependent upon a causal factor, it would be impermanent; therefore, sound is impermanent.
The treatise replies:
This objection is inverted.
Why? Because I do not say that impermanence arises from causes; I say that impermanence is manifested by causes.
While others do not yet know it, I establish this as a "revealing cause" (parijñāna-hetu) so that they may come to know it; it is not a "productive cause" (janana-hetu).
Your objection is based on the productive cause, and thus your objection is inverted.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
What you have stated constitutes both a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) and a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), neither of which we accept.
Why is this? Because we do not believe in or delight in the doctrine of eternal persistence; therefore, we maintain this position.
These ten types are called "the refutation by way of the fallacy of parity" (samasama-jāti), for one establishes a fault based on a fallacious inversion.
If a refutation is similar to these, it falls within the category of the fallacy of parity.
2. Regarding the objection based on the meaning being unreal: it is "unreal" because it is false speech.
False speech is that which does not accord with the meaning and lacks any meaning; this is called the objection based on the meaning being unreal.
There are three types of objections regarding the lack of real meaning (*asatyārtha-vighāta*):

first, the objection that reveals the meaning of non-acceptance; second, the objection that reveals the implication of the meaning (*arthāpatti-vighāta*); and third, the objection that reveals the meaning of a counter-example.

First, regarding the objection that reveals the meaning of non-acceptance: to seek further causes within the locus of what has already been established through direct perception is called the objection that reveals the meaning of non-acceptance.
The treatise says:
Sound is impermanent. Why is this so?
Because it arises dependent upon causes and conditions, like a clay vessel; this point has already been established.
The opponent says:
I see that a clay vessel arises dependent upon causes and conditions; for what reason is it impermanent?
If one were to establish that an earthen jar is impermanent without a cause, then sound likewise should not attain permanence by depending on a permanent cause.
The treatise says:
This objection is not valid.
Why is this? Since it has already been fully understood, there is no need to further establish it through causes.
We see directly that earthenware vessels have causes yet are not eternal; why then must one further seek a cause for impermanence?
Therefore, this objection is not valid.

Second, the "objection based on the implication of the meaning" (*arthāpatti-jāti*): when, regarding the point being countered, this very meaning is implied, it is called the objection based on the implication of the meaning.
The treatise says:
There is no self. Why is this?
Because it cannot be manifested, like the son of a barren woman; this point has already been established.
The opponent says:
By the force of this principle, if something can be manifested, it must certainly exist, and if something cannot be manifested, it must certainly not exist.

That which is manifest may be either existent or non-existent; that which is unmanifest should likewise be understood in this way. For example, a fire-wheel, a mirage, and a city of the Gandharvas are manifest, yet they cannot be established as existing.
If that which can be manifested cannot be definitively established as existent, then that which cannot be manifested cannot be definitively established as non-existent.
The treatise states:
This objection is not valid.
What reasoning is there for the claim that this object is ultimately non-existent and thus cannot be manifested?
If it were ultimately non-existent, it would not be an object that can be manifested.
There are two kinds of objects that can be manifested: those that are reached by the meaning (*arthaprāpta*) and those that are not reached by the meaning (*anarthaprāpta*).
Regarding "logical necessity" (*arthāpatti*): if there is rain, there must be clouds; however, if there are clouds, it is not certain, for there may or may not be rain.
One knows fire by means of smoke, but in this case, logical necessity is not necessarily present.
If one sees smoke and knows there is fire, and sees no smoke and knows there is no fire, this principle does not hold.
Why? Because fire is seen in red-hot iron and glowing coals even though there is no smoke.
Therefore, it is demonstrated that the meaning of objects is ultimately unreal.

Furthermore, there are only forms which are designated as a fire-wheel, a mirage, or a city of the Gandharvas; because of the delusion of the senses and the inversion of the mind, these exist in the present life but do not exist in future lives.
Form alone truly exists; it is only when the faculties are deluded and the mind inverted that one occasionally perceives it as existing.
Your objection—that manifest objects do not necessarily exist—is invalid.
Furthermore, I shall employ the son of a barren woman as a definitive analogy to resolve this point.

That which has no manifest location and is ultimately immovable is a thing that definitely does not exist; for example, the son of a barren woman, who has no manifest location and is immovable, is not an appropriate analogy for the self.
Regarding that which cannot be manifested: in locations such as atoms (*paramāṇu*), it may be manifested or unmanifested.
According to your position, when my position reaches its limit, that which can be manifested remains ultimately immovable; this entity must certainly exist.

Regarding the fire-wheel and other such illusions, it is merely that the wheel is indeterminate; as for this indeterminacy of the wheel, it exists at the time of its rotation but does not exist at the time of its stillness. Therefore, this is not a case of "reaching the meaning" (arthāpatti).
Your objection, which claims that what is not a logical consequence (anarthāpatti) is indeed a logical consequence, is an unreal objection.

Furthermore, another person may state a logical consequence objection as follows: "If sound is impermanent because it shares the same characteristics as a clay pot due to the force of logical necessity (arthāpatti), then if it did not share those characteristics, it would necessarily be permanent."
As for their difference: sound is grasped by the ear and is without form (*amūrta*), whereas a clay vessel is grasped by the eye and possesses form.
Since these characteristics are different, sound is eternal.
The treatise says:

If one objects in this manner, it is a "difficulty regarding the meaning of the common characteristic" (*sādharmya-dūṣaṇa*). Since the difficulty has no distinct essence apart from the meaning [it addresses], I do not accept it.

Third, as for the "difficulty regarding the meaning of the counter-example" (*pratyudāharaṇārtha-dūṣaṇa*): because the meaning is established through the power of the counter-example, this is called the "difficulty regarding the meaning of the counter-example."
The opponent says:

If sound is impermanent because it shares the same characteristic as impermanent vessels, then I shall likewise demonstrate that it is permanent; for sound is permanent because it shares the same characteristic as the permanent ether (*ākāśa*).
If that which possesses the same characteristic as the eternal cannot be eternal, why is it that that which possesses the same characteristic as the impermanent is impermanent?
The treatise says:
This objection is not valid.
Why is this? Only the absence of a thing is called "emptiness. If there were a thing that existed eternally, then this analogy would be established and the objection would also be real.
Since no thing exists eternally, emptiness—being the absence of a thing—cannot be said to be eternal, nor can it be said to be non-eternal; thus, this objection fails as an analogy.
Because using what is not an analogy as an analogy, this objection is unreal.
If one believes that there is a thing called "emptiness" which is eternal, this is a perverse objection, not an objection based on the true meaning.
Why is this? Because that which is bodiless is not fixed.
Emptiness is bodiless and eternally abiding; whereas the mind, suffering, pleasure, desire, and so forth, though bodiless, are impermanent.
Since sound has no physical body, is it permanent like space, or is it impermanent like the mind and so forth?
Having no physical body is indeterminate and cannot serve as a valid reason; therefore, this objection is inverted.
Furthermore, sound is impermanent because it has a cause.
If a thing has a cause, it is known to be impermanent, just like a clay pot and so forth; this point has already been established.
The opponent says:
This meaning is questionable.
Why? Because the arising of a vessel has a cause and is impermanent, whereas the cessation of a vessel has a cause and is permanent.
Since sound has a cause, doubt arises regarding it: does it have a cause and be impermanent like the production of a vessel, or does it have a cause and be permanent like the destruction of a vessel?
The treatise says:
This objection is not valid.

Why is this? There is no real entity that can be called "destruction," for it is only when an object is broken and destroyed by striking with a staff or other means that it acquires the designation "permanent.
Furthermore, sound is impermanent.
Why is this? Because it is grasped by the sense faculties, just like a clay vessel; thus, this point is established.
The opponent says:
This is also questionable: if that which is grasped by the sense faculties were like "sameness" (sāmānya) or "difference" (viśeṣa), it would have to be eternal.
If sound were like that which is grasped by the auditory faculty—namely, like "sameness" or "difference"—then sound would have to be eternal.
If the universal and the particular were not eternal, then the pot would not be impermanent.
The treatise says:
This objection is not valid.

Why is this? If the commonality and difference (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) of cows and so forth were substantially existent as something separate from the cows themselves, there would have to be a distinct entity that could be grasped and perceived.
However, apart from the commonality and difference of cows, no such entity can be grasped or perceived, nor does it possess a separate essence. Therefore, one knows that they are impermanent.
Furthermore, there is no self.
Why? Because it cannot be manifested, just like a snake’s ear; this point has already been established.
The opponent says:
"The number of drops in the ocean and the weight of the Snowy Mountains exist, yet they cannot be manifested.
I am likewise existent, yet cannot be manifested; therefore, because of this reason of non-manifestation, one cannot establish the non-existence of a self."
The treatise says:

Number and quantity have no separate essence from the collection [of atoms]. It is this collection, which is capable of being numbered, that manifests sequentially as "this many" or "that many"; these are the names—such as one, ten, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand, and so forth—established for the purpose of maintaining mindfulness.
Since the measure of a drop of water and the weight of a mountain have no distinct substance, they are not substantially existent.
If there is another objection that shares the same characteristics as this objection, establishing such a fault is called an "objection based on the lack of real meaning" (asiddhārthodbhāvana).
3. Regarding the objection of contradiction (*viruddha-ākṣepa*): when two meanings cannot coexist, it is termed "contradiction.
For example, light and darkness, or sitting and rising, cannot coexist; this is called the objection of contradiction.
There are three types of objections based on contradiction (*viruddha-ākṣepa*):
first, the objection regarding that which has not yet arisen; second, the objection regarding permanence; and third, the objection regarding contradiction with one's own thesis.

First, the objection regarding that which has not yet arisen (*anutpanna-ākṣepa*) is as follows: if, prior to its arising, it were unrelated to causal effort (*yatna*), it would necessarily be permanent; this is the objection regarding that which has not yet arisen.
The opponent says:
"If sound is impermanent because it depends upon effort, then before it has been produced—and thus does not yet depend upon effort—sound should be permanent.
The treatise says:
This objection is contradictory.
Why? Because sound does not yet exist when it has not been produced; how can that which does not yet exist be permanent?
If someone were to say:
"The son of a barren woman is black; his daughter is white," this proposition would likewise have to be established as valid.
If it does not exist, it cannot be permanent; if it is permanent, it cannot be non-existent.
For that which is non-existent yet permanent is self-contradictory.
This objection is similar to the *arthāpatti* (presumption) objection and the *asiddha* (unestablished) objection.
Why is this? Because it is not truly difficult.
Since the proposition that sound is impermanent due to its dependence on effort has already been established, this meaning follows as a logical consequence (*arthāpatti*).
If it did not depend upon effort, it would have to be eternal; however, this proposition is not true.
Why? Because there are three possibilities for that which does not depend upon effort: it is either eternal, non-eternal, or non-existent.
That which is permanent is like space; that which is impermanent is like lightning and the like; and that which does not exist is like flowers in the sky and the like.
These three types do not depend upon human effort; yet you selectively employ only one kind as being permanent, and for this reason, it is not real.
2. Regarding the "objection based on permanence" (*nitya-khaṇḍana*): Because the permanent is non-permanent, sound is permanent; this is called the objection based on permanence.
The opponent says:
In the state of impermanence, there is always impermanence, because all phenomena do not abandon their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"There is permanence within impermanence; by relying on impermanence, one attains permanence.
The Treatise says:
This meaning is contradictory.
Why is this? If something has already ceased to be impermanent, how could it become permanent?
If someone were to say:
The statement "there is light within darkness" should likewise be established.
If it were not so, your objection would be contradictory and unreal.
Why is this? There is no separate dharma called "impermanence" that could be established as "permanent" in relation to the state of impermanence; for impermanence has no distinct essence.
If a thing that has not yet arisen comes into being, and having arisen, ceases, this is called impermanence.
If impermanence is unreal, then to establish permanence based upon impermanence, that permanence is likewise unreal.

3. The Objection of Contradiction with One’s Own Position (*svārthavirodha*). If one refutes the position of another while one’s own position is thereby undermined, this is called the objection of contradiction with one’s own position.
The treatise says:
"Sound is impermanent because it arises dependent on causes and conditions, just like sprouts and the like. This point has already been established.
The opponent says:
If the reason reaches impermanence, it is identical to impermanence; if it does not reach impermanence, it cannot establish impermanence. Thus, this reason fails to function as a reason.
The treatise states:
If your objection reaches my established thesis and is identical to my own thesis, it cannot refute my position.
If it does not reach my established thesis, it likewise cannot refute my position; rather, your objection would instead refute your own position.
Furthermore, the opponent says:
If the reason comes first and the thesis comes later, the thesis does not yet exist; what kind of reason could this be?
If the thesis comes first and the reason comes later, the thesis is already established; what use would the reason be?
This also does not constitute a valid reason.
The treatise states:
If your objection comes first and my thesis is established later, my thesis does not yet exist; what, then, would you have to object to?
If my thesis is established first and your objection follows later, then since my thesis is already established, what further use is there for your objection?
If you say that because you have already accepted my objection, you take up that very objection to further object against me.
If you make this statement, it is likewise not correct.
Why? Because I have demonstrated that your objection actually refutes your own position; I do not establish my own position by relying on your objection.
If there is another objection that shares the same characteristics as this objection, establishing its fault is termed a "contradictory objection" (*viruddha-ākṣepa*).

The treatise says: There are five kinds of formal objections: first, refuting the intended meaning; second, revealing an unintended meaning; third, revealing a perverted meaning; fourth, revealing a dissimilar meaning; and fifth, revealing that nothing can be established through any rational principle.
The opponent says:
There is a self.
For what reason?
They are assembled for the sake of another, just as bedding and other such items are assembled for the sake of another.
The sense organs, such as the eye, are likewise assembled for the sake of another; since this "other" is the self (ātman), we know that the self exists.
The treatise says:
There is no self. Why is this so?
Because it is definitively impossible to manifest.
If there is an entity that is definitively impossible to manifest, that entity does not exist, just as, for example, a second head on a non-omnipotent person.
A second head cannot be conceived or differentiated within the characteristics of a head, such as color, fragrance, and so forth; therefore, it definitely does not exist.
I am likewise; since I am not manifested through discrimination within the sense faculties such as the eye, I certainly do not exist.
Your assertion that I exist is incorrect.
This is called the refutation of the intended meaning.
Furthermore, if you claim that the characteristic of a self is indistinguishable yet existent, then a second head, which is likewise indistinguishable, should also be existent.
If you do not believe that a second head exists, then I am likewise such that you should not believe in me.
This is called the meaning of manifesting displeasure [with your position].

Furthermore, if you intend to say that because the two are equally indistinguishable, you do not assert "I exist" based on reason, yet you do assert "the second head exists," then it would follow as a logical conclusion that I also do not assert "the second head exists" based on reason, nor do I assert "I exist. Thus, this point is established.
If my thesis is not established, your thesis is likewise not established.
This is called "exposing the inverted meaning.
Furthermore, if you say:
I am non-different from the second head, yet it is not that they do not exist as distinct; otherwise, the fault of non-distinction would fall upon your own head, just as if someone were to say:
"The son of a barren woman possesses ornaments."
The statement that "the son of a barren woman has no ornaments" should also be established.
If you make such a claim, you fall into the fault of inconsistency; you are just like this.
This is called clarifying the meaning of their difference.
Furthermore, if you say:
"It is not based on reason that there definitely exists a self, nor is it based on reason that there definitely exists a second head."

If this statement were to be established as valid, then all the incoherent speech of the insane and small children would also have to be established as valid—just as, for example, claiming that space is visible, fire is cold, or wind is graspable. These are all the ravings of the insane and do not rely on reason; yet, according to your position, they too would be established.
If they are not established, then your own thesis is likewise not established.
This is called the exposition of the meaning that all [propositions] lack logical validity and thus cannot achieve accomplishment.
3. Chapter on Points of Defeat (Nigrahasthāna), within the Chapter on Counter-Interrogation. Chapter Three: On Points of Defeat. The Treatise states:
There are twenty-two kinds of points of defeat: first, the subversion of one’s own established thesis; second, the adoption of a different thesis;...
